title: Bosveld Citrus grower system: first consultation

segments.text: Morning, everyone. Thank you for having me, and thanks for the coffee, Johan. Um, before we start, there's one thing I need to check with all of you. I'd like to keep a transcript of this meeting so I can write up the requirements properly afterwards. And I use an AI assistant that runs on my own laptop to help me sort through the transcript.
Nothing goes to an outside service. Are you all comfortable with that?
Yeah, that's fine with me.
Yes, no problem. Fine
by me, as long as it doesn't end up
on the internet somewhere. It

won't. It stays on this laptop, and if anyone wants me to stop at any point, just say so. Okay, how was the road this morning, by the way? I came in on the R-71 from Polyquane, and the stop and go at the pass was terrible.
Ag, those road works.
They've been there since Easter. My wife says they're building a new road one spade at a time.
It's worse in the

afternoon. The truck's in. I'll leave early then. Okay, so I've read the email you sent, Johan, but I'd really like to hear it from you in your own words. Maybe start with the co-op itself, and then what made you pick up the phone?
Sure. So, bar-spelled citrus

co-operative. We're in let's idle about 25 kilometers outside T Zanin. We pack citrus for our members, mostly oranges, volentias and navals, then some lemons, and a fair amount of soft citrus, the mandarins. The co-op was started in 1978 by Eleven Farmers.

Amen. And today we've got, uh, about 140 member growers. Some of them are big commercial farms with a few hundred hectares, and some are small growers from the Enkau and Kaua side with five or six hectares. Everybody's fruit comes through the one packhouse here, behind this office.
And
the packhouse runs all year.

No, no. The season is roughly from the end of March with the early mandarins until about the middle of September, when the last volentias go through. Outside of that we do maintenance. We do the books, and we argue about prices. Mostly
we argue about prices. Yeah,

mostly. So what made me pick up the phone? Honestly, it's the growers. They phone us all day. Where's my fruit? What was my pack out? When do I get paid? Why did my bins get downgraded? And we can't answer them quickly, because the information is in. I'd say five different places, and some of it is on paper.
Five
different places. Can you walk me through them? Precious
can do that better than me. She lives in the packhouse.
Yeah, okay. So it starts at the way bridge. A grower's truck comes in or a

contractor's truck with bins on the back. Each bin is about 400 kilos when it's full. Okay. The truck goes over the way bridge, and our clerk writes a delivery ticket. It's a carbon book, three copies. White copy for the grower, pink for the office, yellow stays in the book.
Handwritten. Handwritten. The way bridge has a little computer with the scale program on it.
It's called Waymate, and it prints the weight on a slip. Then the clerk copies the weight onto the ticket, with the grower number, the farm, the orchard block,
the cultivar and the number of bins. So the weight comes from the machine, but everything else is written by hand. Exactly. Then the bins go into the holding area. They get a,

a cardboard tag tied on with the ticket number, and they wait for the line. How long do they wait? It depends. In the peak, sometimes two days. The early mandarins have to go through the greening first, in the rooms at the back, so it can be a while.

The oranges usually go the next day. Okay, and then? Then the bins go onto the line. We've got an optical grader, the arptosaur, that photographs every fruit and sorts it into classes. Class one for export, class two for the local market, and then juice.
The grader's computer makes a report for each batch. A batch is basically one delivery ticket. Right. And the report says how many cartons of each class and the percentages.
That's what we call the pack out. And the report lives on the grader's computer. It lives on the grader's computer. Tanny Marietje in
the office prints them out every afternoon and files them, and then she types the totals into a spreadsheet. My
spreadsheet. Well, it's the co-op spreadsheet, but I built it.
Okay, so Saifo, the spreadsheet is yours. What does it do? So the

spreadsheet is, ah, the heart of the whole thing, unfortunately. Every delivery is a wrap. Marietje types in the ticket from the pink carpet, and then she adds the pack out from the grader report. And then at the end of each month, I use that to work out the advanced payments to the growers.
Advanced
payments meaning.

So in Citrus, you don't get paid the full price when you deliver. The fruit gets exported. It goes on a ship. It gets sold in Radar Dam or wherever. And only months later do we know the final price. So we pay the growers in advance. So much per carton of class one.
So much per carton of class two. A few ram per bin.
M-M-H-M. And then after the season, there's a final pool payment when all the money is in.
Right. So the monthly calculation is the advance, and the pool payment is once a year.
Once a year, usually in February. And that one's a beast. I
can imagine. And the growers, how do they find out what they've been paid and why?

They get a statement. I make it in the spreadsheet, and Marietje prints it and posts it, or emails it to those who have email. Some of them still come and collect it at the office. They like to have a cup of tea with her.
How long after the month ends do they get it?
Um, honestly, three weeks. Sometimes more. Because everything has to be typed first and checked, and then I have to reconcile
with the bank. And that's when
the phone starts ringing.
So the growers are phoning because they don't know where they stand for three, four

weeks? Exactly. And look, I understand them. A small grower with six hectares, that's his whole income for the year. Yes. He delivered 30 bins two weeks ago, and he doesn't know whether they packed out at 80% or 40%. Of course, he's going to
phone. How many calls are we talking about? In the Saison, I'd say, ah, Marietje gets 40, 50

calls a day. And I get the ones about the grading, maybe 10 a day. Those are the angry ones. Why angry? Because when a batch packs out badly, the grower thinks we made a mistake. He thinks his bins got mixed up with someone else's.

And sometimes, to be honest, they did. Because the cardboard tag fell off, or the ticket number was written badly, and someone read a seven as a one. Okay, that's important. How often does that happen? Not often. Maybe, I don't know, two or three times a week in the peak.
But every time it happens, it's a big fight, and it takes a day to sort out. I have to go through the grader reports, and the
tickets, and phone the driver. Let me make sure I've got the picture. A

truck comes in, it goes over the waybridge, the clerk writes a ticket by hand with a wait from waymate. The bins get a cardboard tag, they wait, they go through the optosort grader. The grader report gets printed, Marietje types the ticket and the pack out into Saifo's spreadsheet, and Saifo works out the advance at the end of the month and makes a statement.
That's it.
That's the whole sad story. And the
fifth place, Johan said five. Oh, the QC

lab, sorry. Before a grower picks an orchard, our lab tests samples, the sugar and the acid and the juice percentage to see if the fruit is mature enough for export. Maturely tests, that's on paper too, and the results go to the grower by WhatsApp.
Our QC lady takes a photo of the sheet and sends it. Okay,
and spray records. You mentioned export. Yeah,

that's a sixth place. Now that you mention it, every grower has to give us his spray records before we can pack his fruit for export because the European buyers test for residues. Those are in a lever arch file in my office.
So there's paper and spreadsheets everywhere, and the growers can't see any of
it themselves. That's really helpful. What's the most painful part for you if you had to pick one? The
phone calls her, no wait, the statements her, because if the statements came out in a week, half the phone calls would go away. For me, it's
the typing. Marietje types for what three, four hours a day in the season,
and she's retiring. When?
End of June
next year, right in the middle of the season, which is a whole other problem. That's
a real risk. Is there someone to take over from her? Not
yet. We'll advertise, but nobody else knows that spreadsheet like her and Syfo. She knows every grower by name. She knows whose son is farming now and whose wife does the books. Okay,
so let's talk about what you'd like. If this goes well, a year from now, what's different? The growers

can see their own deliveries and their pack out on their phones the same day or the day after. They get their statements in a few days, not three weeks, and we start answering 50 phone calls a day. Is
there a number you'd want to hit? Fewer calls, faster statements.
Half. If the calls go down by half, I'd be happy. And statements within, let's say, five working days after the month
end. Five working days is tight, but yeah, if I don't have to wait for the typing, it's
possible. Good. I'll write those down as the goals. Precious from the pack house side. On May, it's the tickets.
I want the waybridge to be quicker, and I want the bins to be traceable without a cardboard tag that falls off in the rain. If every bin had a barcode or something,
and you scanned it, then we'd always know whose fruit is on the line. Do the bins have anything on them today? A number is... The bins belong to the growers mostly. Some have
numbers painted on, some don't. The co-op has about, uh, 3,000 of its own bins that we lend out to the small growers, and those have
numbers burnt into the plastic. So putting a permanent label on each bin isn't straightforward. No, that's why I said
barcode or something. Maybe the barcode is on the tag, not on the bin. A plastic tag that you clip on, and it comes back to the waybridge. I don't know, you're the
expert. I'm not sure I'm the expert on bins, but I'll look into what other pack houses do. Let me note that as something to work out together. So scanning a tag at intake,
and again when the bin goes onto the line. Yes, at the tipper where they tip the bins into
the water. That's where we'd scan.
Hi, sorry, sorry. Is
this the system meeting? Joman said half past nine, I think. Or I heard half past nine.
It was nine, Ruan. Come in, sit. Ayesha, this is Ruan. He does our IT.
He's not staff, he's a contractor, but he's here every Wednesday and whenever something breaks. Hi, Ruan.
Nice to meet you. We've just been through how a delivery goes from the waybridge to the statement, and Precious was talking about scanning bins at the tipper.
Ah, okay. Y'all the scanning. Precious has been on about the scanning for a year.
Because it's needed.
No, I agree, I
agree. Juan, it's actually a good moment for you. What's the network like, at the waybridge and at the tipper?

Uh, so, the office and the pack house are on fiber. It came in two years ago and it's okay. You are. But the waybridge is at the gate, about 300 meters from the office, and it's on a wireless link, point to point. When it rains hard, or when there's load shedding and the battery at the gate runs flat, it drops.

The tipper is inside the pack house, so that's fine, the wifi in there is decent. How often does the waybridge drop? In the season, maybe once a week, for an hour or so. So the waybridge has to keep working without the network? It
has to. We cannot stop trucks at the gate. If a truck waits, the fruit sits in the sun, and the next 20 trucks are behind it on the
road. Okay, so the intake has to work offline, and catch up when the link is back. I'll write that as a firm requirement.
Yeah, and to be honest, I can put a bigger battery on the gate, that's not expensive. But the fiber outages I can't fix. Let's
talk about Waymate for a second. Is it something you can get data out of?

Waymate is old. It runs on a Windows PC under the counter at the gate. It writes every weighing to a little database file, and it can export a CSV at the end of the day. That's
useful. And the greater, the Optisort. That's the

problem one. The Optisort was bought in 2019 from the supplier overseas through their agent in Cape Town. Its computer is locked down. The reports come out as PDFs. There might be a database underneath, but we don't have the password, and the agent says if we touch it, we void the support contract.
So getting the pack out of the greater automatically is uncertain. Very
uncertain. I can ask the agent whether they have an export, a CSV, or an API, or something. They might want money for
it. Would you mind asking them? That's probably the biggest unknown we've got.
Loyolas, I'll send them
an email this week. Thank you. And if the answer is no, the fallback is someone typing the totals from the report, which is what Marietji does now. Or

bad ones. Perfect. And on the accounting side, Cypo, what do you use? We

use Ledger 1 for the books. The payments to the Grohl's go out through the bank in a batch file that I upload to the bank's business banking. The spreadsheet makes the batch file, actually. Well, it makes a list, and I copy it into the bank's template. So
the payment calculation is in your spreadsheet, and Ledger 1 gets the totals.
The totals, yeah. I journal them in at the end of the month. Would
you want the new system to calculate the advances, or do you want to keep that in your spreadsheet for now?

Hem, honestly. Keep it in my spreadsheet for now. The rules change every season. The board decides different advance rates for different cultivars and sizes, and I don't want to fold a developer every time the board changes its mind. If the system gives me the deliveries and the packout clean, I'll do the sums.
I agree.
Let's not build the payment engine in the first round.

Okay, so that's a decision. The payment calculation stays in Cypo's spreadsheet for Phase 1, and the new system gives him the deliveries and packout as an export he can open in the spreadsheet. And then the statement. Does the statement come from the new system or from the spreadsheet?
Um, that's
a good question. If the advances worked
out in my spreadsheet, the statement has to show the advance, so either I upload the amounts back
into the system every month, or the statement stays in the spreadsheet. Let's
leave that one open for now. I'll come back with a couple of options. It depends on how much work and upload would be for you each month.
Okay. Can we
talk about the grower's information for a bit? What do you
hold about them?
Names, ID numbers for the growers who farm as individuals. Company registration numbers for the farms that are companies, VAT
numbers, bank account details, physical addresses, phone numbers, email, and their delivery history, their
packouts, and what they've been paid.
Okay, so for the small growers who farm in their own name, that's all personal information under POPIA, and the bank details need care in any case. Who should be able to see what? A

grower must only see his own stuff. That's the number one thing. If grower can see what grower be got paid, I'll have a war on my head. Right. Seriously, these people are neighbors. Their kids go to the same school. They sit next to each other in church.
I
understand. So each grower sees only their own deliveries, packouts and statements, and in the office. Me
and Johan see everything. Marietje sees everything except no. Actually, she sees everything too.
Precious and the clerks need the deliveries and the grading, but not the bank details and not the money.
I don't want to see the money. So the

roles are something like this. The office and management see everything. The packhouse staff see deliveries and grading, but not bank details or payments. And growers see their own. Who changes a grower's bank details today?
Only me. And
only with a letter from the bank. Because there's fraud.
Amen.
Last year someone phoned pretending to be one of our growers and asked us to change his bank account. Luckily Marietje knew his voice.
That's exactly the kind of thing to design for. So changing bank details stays a manual, checked process in the office, and a grower can't change them from their phone.
Definitely not.
Good. And the weights. What if someone changes a weight or a bin count
after the fact? That must be recorded. Who changed it and why? Because that's where the fights are. So an audit trail on every change to a
delivery. Who changed it when, what it was before, and the reason? Yes.
And the grower should be able to see that it was changed, I think. Hum,
maybe not the reason.
Sometimes the reason is, you know, the driver counted wrong because he was in a hurry to get to the bottle store.
Okay, maybe
not the reasons. I'll note that the grower sees that a delivery
was corrected, and whether they also see the reason is still to be decided. Juen, where would all this live? Do you have a preference for hosting?
Not on a server in the office, please. I don't want another thing to look after, and the power here isn't reliable. Some cloud thing is fine. The board
said the data must stay in South Africa. One of our members is a lawyer, and he was very firm about that at the last meeting. Okay,
so hosting in a South African data center. That's a constraint, and it's possible with most of the big providers now. Yeah,
they've got Joe Hansberg in Cape Town regions. Exactly. And
for the weighbridge, the tablet or PC at the gate would keep its own copy of the day's deliveries and send them up when the link is back.
And if the tablet gets stolen?
Good point. Then it should need a PIN or a login, and it shouldn't hold more than it needs. The day's deliveries and the grower list, not bank
details. Okay, that works for me.
How long do you keep the records now? Tickets and statements? The
auditors say
five years for anything financial. The tickets we keep are, I think also five years, in boxes in the store. The mice eat some of
them. Five years then, for deliveries and statements, and when a grower leaves
the co-op. We keep his records for the five years, for tax, and then, honestly, nobody has ever thrown anything

away. That's common. I'll suggest that the system keeps a leaver's records for five years, and then flags them for deletion, and you decide. Let's talk about the growers themselves. How do they use their phones? What kind of

phones? Everything. The big farmers have iPhones and laptops, and their own farm managers. The small growers, a lot of them have cheap Android phones, and data is expensive. Some of them, the older ones, their kids do the phone stuff for them. So
whatever the growers use has to work on a cheap Android phone, on a slow connection, without eating their data.
Yeah, and I don't want them to have to download an app. Last time somebody made us an app, for the, uh, the study group, nobody installed it. 12 people out of 140.
A web page they open from a link, then. One they can save to the home screen, like an
app. That's fine.

And SMS. Not everybody uses WhatsApp properly, but everybody gets SM says. What would you send them? When their batch is graded, your delivery number 4471 packed out at 78% class one, something like that, with
a link to see the
rest. That's a nice one. Johan, are you happy with
SMS? SMS is fine. What's app costs money if you do it through the business? Doesn't it fuel
it? Yeah, it's per message through one of the providers, but SMS also costs about, I think, 25, 30 cents a message.
Then let's say, SMS for the grading notifications to start with, and maybe what's app later. Are you all okay with that?
Yeah, fine.
Good, that's decided. And how does a grower log in? Most of them won't want another
password. No passwords. They'll forget it and phone
us. One option is a code sent by SMS to the phone number you already have on file for them. They type the code and they
are in. It works if the number on file is right. Some of them change their
numbers. Then updating a phone number would go through the office, like the bank details, so nobody can take over someone else's account by changing the number.

rule. Now language. The growers speak.

My mother would want it
in Zitzonga, but she reads English too. Do you want the grower pages translated?

have to be in English for the orders anyway.

one. The PC is under the counter and the clerk has to go inside the little office to use it while the driver waits. Then it

Ruan.

ticket? Yes. The driver must leave with something in his hand, otherwise the grower

phones to ask if the fruit arrived. A small printed slip is fine, like a till's slip. So a small printer next to the tablet, that prints a slip for each grower on the truck. Yours and the SMS too if they want it, but the slip always.
The old ones like paper.
And if the tablet itself breaks on a busy morning. We keep the carbon books in the drawer, just in case, then someone types them in afterwards. That's sensible. I'll make sure there's a
quick way to enter the paper tickets afterwards, so nothing gets lost. Y'all
keep the books. Tablets always die at the worst moment. Okay,
let's talk volumes. How many trucks
